newsitem.title: USA: WHEAT--U.S. HRW growers face ideal sowing weather.
newsitem.headline: WHEAT--U.S. HRW growers face ideal sowing weather.

text.p: U.S. hard red winter wheat growers faced near-ideal sowing weather this week after weekend storms dropped several inches of rain across the central U.S. Plains, agronomists said.

"The prospects look real good," said Mark Hodges, executive director of the Oklahoma Wheat Commission. "There's plenty of surface moisture and plenty of subsurface moisture to plant in -- assuming (growers) can get into the fields."
Hodges noted that recent rains had been heavy enough to cause planting to lag the five-year average.

During the week ended Sunday, 10 percent of Oklahoma's wheat acreage had been seeded, behind 12 percent last year and the 20-percent average, according to the Oklahoma Agricultural Statistics Service.

Hodges said western Oklahoma and particularly the Panhandle had received so much rainfall throughout the summer that weeds were posing a considerable problem to producers trying to prepare their fields for seeding.
"There's still producers that are trying to get their fields in condition to plant," Hodges said.
Hodges said that the ideal time to plant wheat for grain in central Oklahoma was during the first week in October.
But he noted that 50 percent of the state's wheat acreage was usually earmarked for grazing, and he said planting of this acreage had started in early September.

The most recent crop progress report rated Oklahoma's topsoil moisture condition as 11 percent short, 81 percent adequate and eight percent surplus -- a far cry from the extremely short moisture conditions that resulted from the drought earlier this year.

The current moisture situation was similar in Kansas, traditionally the largest U.S. winter wheat producer. During the week ended Sunday, Kansas' topsoil moisture was rated one percent very short, 24 percent short, 72 percent adequate and three percent surplus.
Six percent of the state's wheat acreage was seeded, ahead of five percent last year but lagging the 12-percent average.
"You got a good moist seedbed... so things are looking pretty decent for planting anyway," said Stu Duncan, Kansas State University extension specialist in crops and soils for south central Kansas.
Duncan said memories of last year's dryness spurred some farmers into planting ahead of schedule, which could cause some wheat to develop too early.
"I think some of them did plant early, and we'll have to see what happens. It makes no sense -- all they do is remember what happened last year," Duncan said.

In Nebraska, another leading U.S. HRW wheat producer, 25 percent of the state's wheat acreage was planted as of Sunday, compared to 11 percent during the previous week, 32 percent last year and the average of 36 percent.
